name: Panama
note: Traveler-focused Panama pack (civil-law country). For visitors: emergencies, police/ID, if detained, drugs, driving, entry/exit, tenancy. Verify before relying; laws change and this is not local legal advice.

resources.name: Your embassy / consulate
resources.note: If detained, demand consular contact. Save your country's 24h emergency line before you travel.

resources.name: Tourist Police (Policía de Turismo)
resources.note: Operate in visitor areas and can assist tourists.

getLawyer.why: In Panama, if you are arrested or detained, you have the right to contact your embassy/consulate — do that immediately (Canada/US/UK consulates can help find a local lawyer and monitor your treatment). Do not sign anything you don't understand; ask for an interpreter and a lawyer.

Panama treats drug possession and trafficking very severely — heavy fines and long prison sentences, with pre-trial detention common. Contact your embassy and a local lawyer immediately; say nothing without counsel.
Emergency numbers in Panama: 104 (police), 911 (medical), 103 (fire). If you're in danger call now. For anything legal, contact your embassy's emergency line.

deadlines.title: Tourist stay — up to 180 days
deadlines.rule: Most visitors (incl. Canada/US/EU) may stay visa-free up to 180 DAYS. To stay longer you must change status; to 'renew' as a tourist you must leave for at least 30 days, and re-entry can be refused. Overstaying brings fines and exit problems.
deadlines.source: Government of Canada travel advice — Panama

deadlines.title: Entry stamp required on arrival
deadlines.rule: You must obtain an entry stamp on arrival; failing to have one can bring a US$1,000 fine on exit. You may also need to show onward/return travel and proof of funds (≈US$500 or a credit card).
deadlines.source: Government of Canada travel advice — Panama

deadlines.title: Foreign licence valid ~90 days
deadlines.rule: A foreign driver's licence is generally valid for up to 90 DAYS; carry an international driving permit too. Insurance is mandatory. After an accident, call police and do NOT move the vehicle until an officer says so.
deadlines.source: Government of Canada travel advice — Panama

sentencing.name: Drug possession / trafficking (Panama)
sentencing.mandatory_minimum: Pre-trial detention is common; penalties are severe.
sentencing.first_offender: Even small amounts can mean prison and long pre-trial detention for foreigners; outcomes vary and a local lawyer is essential.

statutes.title: Must carry ID at all times
statutes.summary: Panamanian law requires everyone to carry official identification (passport or a certified copy) at all times; you can be fined or detained if you cannot produce it.

statutes.title: Right to consular access when detained
statutes.summary: A detained foreign national has the right to have their consulate notified and to communicate with it — ask for this immediately if arrested.

book.title: Police, ID, and if you're detained in Panama
book.overview: Panama is a civil-law country. As a visitor the most important things: always carry ID, be calm and polite with police (including the tourist police in visitor areas), and if you're ever detained, contact your embassy immediately. Emergency numbers: 104 police, 911 medical, 103 fire.
your_rights: You must carry official ID (passport or certified copy) at all times — not having it can mean a fine or detention.
If detained or arrested, you have the right to contact your embassy/consulate and to a lawyer and interpreter.
Do not sign documents you don't understand; ask for a translation and legal help.
Tourist police operate in visitor areas and can assist.
You have the right not to be mistreated — report problems to your consulate.
key_steps: Carry ID always; keep a photo/copy of your passport separately.
Stay calm and cooperative; don't argue roadside — resolve issues through a lawyer/consulate.
If detained: ask to contact your embassy and a lawyer; say little until then.
Save emergency numbers: 104 / 911 / 103, and your embassy's 24-hour line.
Keep proof of your entry stamp and status.
common_mistakes: Arguing with or filming police confrontationally.
Signing Spanish-language documents without understanding them.
Not contacting the embassy early when detained.
book.when_lawyer: If detained, arrested, or in any drug matter: contact your embassy immediately and get a local lawyer — don't wait. For minor issues, the tourist police or your embassy can point you to help.

book.title: Entry, tourist stay, and overstaying in Panama
book.overview: Most visitors get up to 180 days visa-free, but you must get an entry stamp on arrival and may need to show onward travel and proof of funds. Overstaying or missing your stamp causes fines and exit problems.
your_rights: Visa-free tourist stays of up to 180 days for many nationalities (incl. Canada/US/EU).
You can extend by changing status; 'renewing' as a tourist requires leaving for 30+ days, and re-entry isn't guaranteed.
You're entitled to your entry stamp — insist on it on arrival.
key_steps: Get and keep your entry stamp (missing it can cost US$1,000 on exit).
Carry proof of onward/return travel and funds (≈US$500 or a credit card).
For longer stays, consult a Panamanian immigration lawyer about residency.
common_mistakes: Overstaying and facing fines at the airport.
Assuming a quick border hop resets your tourist time.
book.when_lawyer: For residency, work status, or an overstay problem, see a Panamanian immigration lawyer; your embassy can provide a list.

book.title: Getting arrested or charged in Panama (esp. drugs)
book.overview: Panama's criminal process is different from common-law countries, pre-trial detention is common, and drug offences are punished severely. The essentials: contact your embassy, get a local lawyer, and say nothing without counsel and an interpreter.
your_rights: Right to contact your embassy/consulate and a lawyer.
Presumption of innocence, but pre-trial detention is common — a lawyer is essential to seek release.
key_steps: Immediately ask to contact your embassy and a lawyer.
Do not sign or admit anything without counsel and translation.
Have someone notify family and your embassy's emergency line.
Keep calm; cooperate procedurally but don't give statements without a lawyer.
common_mistakes: Talking to police without a lawyer/interpreter.
Any involvement with drugs — penalties are severe.
Not using the embassy, which can monitor and refer lawyers.
book.when_lawyer: Immediately — a local Panamanian criminal lawyer, with your embassy's help. For drugs, treat it as an emergency.

book.title: Emergencies and staying safe in Panama
book.overview: For any emergency in Panama: 104 police, 911 medical, 103 fire. Avoid known higher-risk areas (parts of Colón, the Darién region, some Panama City neighbourhoods at night), use registered taxis/rideshare, and keep your embassy's emergency number handy.
your_rights: You can call emergency services (104/911/103) and seek police help.
Your embassy has a 24-hour emergency line for citizens in distress.
You can report crimes to police and get a report for insurance.
key_steps: Save 104 / 911 / 103 and your embassy's emergency number.
After a crime, report to police and get a written report.
Avoid displaying valuables; use hotel safes and registered transport.
In danger, call emergency services first, then your embassy.
common_mistakes: Not knowing the local emergency numbers.
Resisting a robbery (hand over valuables; safety first).
Not getting a police report for insurance claims.
book.when_lawyer: For injury, a serious crime against you, or any detention, contact your embassy; they can refer local lawyers.
